title: Plugging In, Charging Ahead: Comparing EU and Canadian Approaches to Chinese Investment in the Electric Vehicle Sector
text:
Executive Summary

This paper compares the divergent strategies of the European Union (EU) and Canada as they navigate Chinese investment in their respective electric vehicle (EV) sectors. Both jurisdictions seek to maximize local economic benefits, decarbonize, and strengthen industrial competitiveness, but their tactical mechanisms differ. While some EU member states initially welcomed investments, the EU is now shifting toward a rules-based model that would place strict conditions on Chinese investment, centering on the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) and complementing it with measures on supply chain diversification and cybersecurity. Canada, by contrast, has emphasized political signaling and pragmatic flexibility. After dropping prohibitive tariffs in exchange for importing a limited number of Chinese EVs with minimal tariffs, Ottawa has sought to leverage market access to incentivize Chinese firms to “build where you sell.” Officials have emphasized political engagement and a set of four guiding principles to court majority Canadian-owned joint ventures, though no concrete deals have yet been approved. Ultimately, both approaches are a work in progress, with Beijing’s tightening controls on outbound investment, China’s level of market access, and regional trade uncertainties likely to shape outcomes.

Introduction

In mid-June, Canadian Industry Minister Mélanie Joly traveled to Shanghai. The official news release for her trip deployed a politely diplomatic phrase, “advance commercial opportunities with appropriate guardrails,” to describe a core objective of Joly’s visit: attracting Chinese investment in Canada’s electric vehicle (EV) sector on Canadian terms. Her packed schedule included site visits and meetings with four Chinese EV makers—an agenda that would have seemed improbable just six months earlier, before Canada replaced 100% tariffs on Chinese EVs with a quota to import a limited number of EVs annually with minimal tariffs. That deal was part of a broader bargain that included Beijing rolling back steep retaliatory duties on Canadian canola and other agricultural exports and Ottawa seeking to attract greater local investment.While Joly toured BYD’s Changzhou production site and a Geely research and development center, relations between the European Union (EU) and China simmered near the boiling point. Against the backdrop of the EU’s surging trade deficit and the EU Commission’s opening several new antidumping investigations into Chinese goods, Chinese officials hastily canceled two high-level meetings with EU counterparts in early June. Only when Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao visited Brussels in late June did both sides finally agree to set up a formal mechanism to monitor trade flows in a fragile bid to avoid a full-blown trade war, with the EU setting a deadline for “tangible results” by October when the EU trade chief is set to visit Beijing. Prior to that meeting, EU leaders had directed the European Commission to develop new trade instruments to defend EU interests.Canada and the EU are grappling with their long-term approaches to Chinese investment, with the EV sector at the heart of their respective strategies. Both are driven by the same objective of shaping commercial engagement with China in ways that maximize domestic economic benefits and strengthen industrial competitiveness amid growing trade imbalances, while advancing vehicle electrification, energy security, and decarbonization. The Strait of Hormuz energy crisis has reinforced the urgency of the challenge: amid fuel price volatility and supply insecurity, consumer demand for EVs has skyrocketed; relying primarily on imported Chinese vehicles, despite their low cost and strong performance, could further decimate domestic industries. Given the two geographies started from different baselines, their strategies have diverged, though both are a work in progress.The EU has focused on conditioning Chinese investment by leveraging the pull of its domestic market, moving away from a relatively open investment model and toward a more restrictive framework. The centerpiece of this strategy is the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which introduces new controls on EVs and other cleantech investments of more than €100 million (US$114 million) from countries with a dominant market share—effectively China—to revitalize Europe’s industrial base and align decarbonization with economic security. Additional policies aim to tighten investment screening, diversify supply chains, and improve cybersecurity controls. In that sense, EU tactics have emphasized strict conditions, hoping the resulting rules mold investment outcomes that serve EU interests.Canada, by contrast, has placed greater emphasis on political signaling and pragmatic flexibility. Compared to the EU, Canada is in a relatively nascent stage of efforts to attract Chinese investment in the EV industry, which have only gained meaningful momentum since the EV quota replaced tariffs in January 2026. Rather than legislating requirements, so far, Joly has raised four guiding conditions that proposed Chinese investments should meet, while actively engaging with Chinese automakers to court favorable investments following Prime Minister Mark Carney’s deal. Since Canada initially followed the United States in adopting high tariffs to limit Chinese market access, it is attempting to use its relative lack of Chinese investment to incentivize partnerships that might invigorate its economy in the face of U.S. trade pressures. Some in Ottawa may also see the prospect of Chinese investment as a source of leverage in negotiations with Washington over the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) review and other bilateral tariff issues, although U.S. officials have accused Canada of sending mixed messages by seeking Chinese investment while pledging to support North American reindustrialization.Apart from tactics, equally significant is the political message that each jurisdiction’s approach sends to Beijing. The EU’s proposed conditions signal to prospective Chinese investors that while the EU market will remain open, future investments may become more bureaucratically challenging and unwieldy. Canada, conversely, has so far welcomed investment while outsourcing the details to companies. Although this has encouraged some firms to actively make offers, Ottawa has retained final approval authority, and no investments have moved forward to date. Some in Canada have also called for the government to pursue more detailed conditions.Ultimately, outcomes will depend on Chinese companies’ willingness to invest and whether Beijing permits them to do so. It is still unclear how recent Chinese policies that aim to control outbound investment and secure supply chains will interact with host countries’ desired terms, especially around sensitive areas such as technology transfer. Despite widespread interest from foreign players to gain advanced technologies from Chinese firms, substantive evidence of technology transfer remains limited in practice.Both the EU and Canada are in the early stages of pursuing their respective approaches to Chinese EV investment. It will take some time for the dust to settle on broader outcomes, and both jurisdictions’ strategies may further evolve. Nevertheless, analyzing these two economies’ approaches and the responses they have elicited so far from Chinese stakeholders could shed light on the relative effectiveness of different tactics. It can also provide important lessons for the United States and other economies that are facing similar challenges.

The EU: From member state discretion to conditional strings attached

The EU did not initially adopt a comprehensive framework for scrutinizing Chinese investment on broader economic or industrial policy grounds. Following a wave of investments, the EU established its Foreign Direct Investment Screening Regulation in 2019, which created a mechanism for coordinating national reviews of foreign investments affecting security or public order. Recent updates to the regulation mandate that all member states adopt screening mechanisms by 2028, rather than just encouraging them, and strengthen provisions around sensitive sectors. The 2023 Foreign Subsidies Regulation also empowered the European Commission to address distortive foreign subsidies. While the Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI) concluded in 2020 would have required both the EU and Chinese markets to eliminate various investment conditions, it was never ratified following the deterioration of EU-China relations in 2021.Decisions about whether to attract, approve, or condition most foreign investments, therefore, remain primarily with member states. As a result, Chinese firms have already established a significant presence across a range of sectors in certain member states, including in clean technology sectors. In 2025, Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) into Europe reached its highest level since 2018 at €16.8 billion (US$19.1 billion). Nearly half of that figure flowed into the automotive sector and EV supply chains.The EU’s approach began to shift as concerns grew over Europe's severe and growing trade imbalance with China and its ability to capture the economic benefits of these investments while reducing strategic dependencies. Using tools intended to offset unfair subsidies, the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs ranging from 7.8% to 35.3% in 2024. Following pressure from China, in January 2026, the European Commission opened a pathway for Chinese EV exporters to seek relief from the EU’s countervailing duties by offering minimum-price commitments instead. Those offers are being considered individually, with only Volkswagen’s Cupra receiving approval so far; no broader EU-China deal has been reached, leaving the tariffs largely still in place. At the same time, rather than preventing Chinese investment outright, policymakers have increasingly focused on shaping the terms under which it occurs.At the center of the EU’s investment strategy is the IAA, a legislative proposal introduced by the European Commission in March 2026 that aims to boost domestic manufacturing, accelerate industrial decarbonization, and reduce strategic dependencies on foreign suppliers. For investments in “emerging strategic sectors” such as EVs, the IAA would require prior authorization when the investment exceeds €100 million (US$114 million) and the investor comes from a country that controls more than 40% of global manufacturing capacity in that sector—a threshold widely understood as aimed principally at China. Qualifying investments would be required to fulfill specific conditions, which include limits on foreign ownership, joint ventures with European partners, technology transfer, EU-based research and development, local sourcing, and domestic employment commitments. The proposal still requires approval by the European Parliament and Council, and adoption is not expected before 2027.Complicating this process, though, are the differing interests and perspectives from member states, which may limit the speed and efficacy of the proposal’s adoption and eventual implementation. A key debate centers on whether the policy should prioritize products “Made in Europe” or those “Made by Europe.” Some governments—led by France—have championed the latter, arguing that European industries need protection in the face of cheaper imports from China and other markets with looser environmental and other regulations. But others, including Sweden and the Czech Republic, have warned that "buy local" requirements could deter investment, raise prices in government tenders, and hurt the EU's global competitiveness.Beyond the IAA, the EU is also considering other instruments to diversify supply chains and reduce reliance on China. Another policy that has been floated would set ceilings, expected to be about 30% to 40%, for what can be bought from a single supplier. Remaining components would need to be sourced from at least three suppliers, not all from the same country—a structure aimed squarely at diversifying supplies away from China. Though a formal proposal has yet to be submitted or clarified if the EV sector would be covered, this could complicate vertical integration for EU-based firms, including Chinese-invested facilities, and prompt businesses to prioritize supply diversification above factors including cost and efficiency.In addition, under proposed revisions to its Cybersecurity Act, the EU plans to phase out components and equipment from "high-risk" suppliers in critical sectors, which are likely to include EVs. While the designation is not country specific, Chinese firms are widely expected to be among the primary targets due to long-standing concerns regarding cybersecurity vulnerabilities, data security, and potential foreign government influence. The measures are likely to affect EVs and other sectors deemed essential to economic and national security, such as telecommunications, energy, transportation, and digital infrastructure.Chinese officials contest policies as overly restrictive, while Chinese firms frontload investment in welcoming marketsIn the face of diverging member state views, which may water down and delay the adoption of the IAA and other measures, Chinese officials have pushed back on the EU’s proposed investment conditions. China’s Ministry of Commerce has publicly criticized the IAA, which heavily promotes "Made in Europe" self-reliance and restricts foreign investment in strategic sectors, labeling it discriminatory and a violation of fair competition principles. China has also raised its concerns in the World Trade Organization (WTO), arguing that the IAA’s "Made in Europe" mandate creates systemic discrimination against Chinese cleantech and strategic sectors.On the revisions to the Cybersecurity Act, Beijing ⁠wants clauses that define "countries posing cybersecurity concerns" and "high risk" to be dropped from the proposed rules. In early May, officials threatened countermeasures against the EU if substantial changes were not made. According to China's Chamber of Commerce to the EU, should the proposal phase out equipment from Chinese suppliers, it could cost the bloc more than $400 billion in the next five years due to efficiency losses and other challenges from replacing hardware and writing down assets, with Germany facing nearly half of ‌the burden.In the meantime, Chinese companies are continuing to pursue commercial interests in the EU. In 2025, Chinese FDI hit a seven-year high. The automotive sector attracted the most investment, totaling €7.6 billion (US$8.6 billion)—a 46% increase from 2024—with 93% focused on the EV supply chain. Most investments are concentrated in markets that offer a political welcome, including Hungary, which attracted €3.8 billion (US$4.3 billion) in 2025; Spain, where FDI increased by 147%; and Germany, which saw investment rise 88%. If the IAA is adopted, those firms that invest now could gain a competitive advantage in the EU market compared to those that may later be subject to its strict conditions.Hungary was an early favorite destination during former prime minister Viktor Orban’s tenure. In 2022, CATL officially announced it would invest €7.34 billion (US$8.3 billion) to build a 100GWh battery plant in eastern Hungary with the goal of providing batteries for the European market. EV giant BYD also built its first European passenger car plant in Hungary to assemble electric vehicles locally. Trial production commenced in early 2026, with complete vehicle assembly slated to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026. While Budapest is likely to be more circumspect toward Beijing under opposition leader and now prime minister Péter Magyar, existing Chinese investments are likely to stay.More recently, Chinese companies have rushed toward Spain, especially after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez vocally welcomed Chinese investment during his April 2026 trip to Beijing. Already in 2024, Stellantis and CATL had formed a joint venture to build an all-new lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery plant at Stellantis's Zaragoza site, with production slated to begin at the end of 2026. Additionally, Chery entered into a €400 million (US$456 million) EV joint venture with EV Motors in Barcelona. During Sánchez’s Beijing trip, Hithium made a deal to build its first European battery storage gigafactory in the country. Since then, SAIC Motor has confirmed it will build its first EV plant in Galicia, and wind company MingYang is reportedly eyeing Spain after the UK rejected a proposed investment.In addition to frontloading investments, Chinese companies have explored creative workarounds to expand access to the European market, especially through contract manufacturing. Ford, Nissan, and Volkswagen have all held discussions with Chinese firms, such as Geely and BYD, regarding the use of idle capacity at European plants, as they wrestle with sluggish demand and high production costs. Geely is already using part of Ford's plant near Valencia to produce vehicles for the European market, a move that allows it to avoid the high tariffs on shipments from China.Even with these trends, the status of Chinese-invested facilities in Europe is still relatively nascent. In the EV sector, the earliest Chinese investments are only just nearing the start of production: BYD’s €3.8 billion (US$4.3 billion) plant in Szeged, Hungary, is reportedly close to operation, with full-scale production slated for the end of 2026, and Stellantis-Leapmotor is set to produce the Leapmotor B10 at its Zaragoza, Spain, plant starting in the second half of 2026. As a result, key questions remain, including how demand for locally manufactured vehicles will compare with demand for imported models, to what extent countries that attracted Chinese investment will derive benefits, and what this will all mean for the balance between local production and trade.

Canada: Using political signaling and guiding principles to attract deals

Canada initially aligned itself closely with Washington's broader effort to limit Chinese automotive penetration of the North American market. After President Joe Biden’s May 2024 imposition of 100% tariffs on Chinese EVs, Ottawa followed suit with its own 100% tariffs in August of that year under former prime minister Justin Trudeau. However, as Canada faced mounting economic uncertainty and growing trade pressure from the United States, it recently started to shift toward a more transactional and diversified model that attempts to leverage limited market access to incentivize local investment.Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s visit to Beijing in January 2026 was hailed as a landmark shift in Sino-Canadian relations after several years of tense exchanges. During the trip, Canada agreed to admit 49,000 Chinese EVs at a most-favored-nation (MFN) tariff rate of 6.1%, accounting for roughly 3% of Canada’s overall vehicle market—a provision agreed to in exchange for Beijing slashing its retaliatory tariffs on Canadian canola seed from roughly 84% to about 15% and easing curbs on other agricultural exports. Importantly, the EV quota included provisions for at least half of imported vehicles to be “affordable,” or less than $35,000 CAD (US$24,900), by 2030. It is also set to expand by 6.5% per year to a maximum of 70,000 vehicles annually by the same date. The quota took effect on March 1, 2026, for an initial six-month period, while the Canadian government sought public input on a longer-term allocation system to begin September 1.The official announcement of the deal also clarified that Carney’s ultimate objective was not just opening its market but also attracting investment: “We expect that this will catalyze considerable new Chinese joint venture investments in Canada with trusted partners to protect and create new auto manufacturing jobs for Canadian workers and ensure a robust build-out of Canada's EV supply chain.” In contrast to the EU, Canada has yet to introduce a comprehensive, rules-based framework toward Chinese automotive investment. Under the Investment Canada Act (ICA), a federal law governing large FDI in Canada since the 1980s, the Canadian federal government reviews FDI above certain thresholds to ensure they are of “net benefit to Canada.” Furthermore, foreign investments of any size could be reviewed on national security grounds and potentially blocked if they are deemed to be harmful to Canada’s national security.For the time being, Minister Joly has put forward four guiding principles for investments to be approved:Be a joint venture that is majority Canadian owned;Apply labor standards aligned with those in Canada’s existing auto industry;Source from localized supply chains and Canadian suppliers; andUse secure vehicle software and protect users’ data.These guidelines have established expectations for investments that seek to move forward while leaving significant room for interpretation and negotiation, given that detailed thresholds or binding requirements have not yet been provided. Certain categories of conditions are also conspicuously missing from the list. For example, technology transfer and licensing of intellectual property—which have received significant attention in the EU and are incorporated into the IAA’s conditions—have not been emphasized by Joly in her public-facing messaging. It also remains to be seen how contract manufacturing, which adopts a different cooperative structure than a majority-Canadian joint venture, might be treated. Ultimately, Canada’s ICA framework provides the government with the authority to approve or block investments.The combination of Joly’s political signaling regarding desired investment structures with a legislated system for federal approval of investments provides some degree of flexibility regarding how individual conditions are interpreted. However, it cannot necessarily solve for broader uncertainties. Ottawa’s ambitions may be tempered by union opposition, which is driven by concerns over domestic jobs and industrial competitiveness and may constrain support for deeper engagement with Chinese automakers. Another critical open question is whether Canada will be able to export domestically produced vehicles from foreign-invested factories to its desired end markets, especially the United States.Chinese firms signal their interest but hesitate to invest amid regional trade uncertaintyAfter the initial announcement in January, Chinese companies including BYD, Chery, and Geely began laying the groundwork to sell vehicles in Canada. On the trade front, Chinese-produced EVs started arriving in Canada in May. Thus far, most appear to be from Western brands operating in China, such as Tesla, so it remains to be seen how Canadian consumers will react to Chinese brands’ more prominent arrival. Tesla had already prepared in 2023 by equipping its Shanghai Gigafactory to produce a Canada-specific version of the Model Y, although the company halted those shipments and shifted Canadian supply to its U.S. and Berlin factories after Ottawa’s 2024 imposition of the 100% tariff.Given Canada’s expressed preference to import vehicles from companies that also produce locally, some Chinese firms have put forth proposals regarding local production. Canadian officials have reacted to individual proposals on a case-by-case basis, especially toward those investment models that they believe would not necessarily advance Ottawa’s objectives.As one example, Stellantis suggested partnering with Chinese automaker Leapmotor, which it partially owns, to assemble electric vehicles using "knock-down kits", or pre-manufactured vehicle components shipped unassembled for final assembly in the destination country at its idled plant in Brampton, Ontario. Minister Joly ruled out this model, stating that plans must be supported by the provincial government and the workers’ union. Separately, BYD’s Executive Vice President Stella Li said that she does not believe a joint venture would work due to the company’s vertical integration and that BYD would insist on owning and operating any Canadian facility outright. However, Canadian officials have articulated their desire for joint ventures, making it unclear whether a wholly owned BYD factory could feasibly move forward.Ahead of her June China trip, Joly reiterated that Chinese automakers would need to “build where you sell.” In doing so, she referenced the need to adhere to the aforementioned four conditions. Joly has also suggested she wants to see Canadian companies engaged in contract manufacturing for Chinese EV makers in Canadian factories or plants, such as what Magna International does for China’s Xpeng in Austria. Analysts have noted that this model is not a joint venture and centers instead on assembly, rather than substantive technology or IP transfer, reflecting potential inconsistency in Joly’s messaging.Following her June meetings with representatives from BYD, Chery, Geely, and Shanghai Launch Automotive Technology, Joly implied that progress was made in persuading Chinese automakers to set up shop in Canada. Yet, despite expressions of interest, no major Chinese automotive investment in Canada has formally moved forward. One reason is that Canada has only been courting Chinese investment for about half a year, so it is still relatively early. Another important factor is ambiguity surrounding the fate of the USMCA, as the value of locating production in Canada depends heavily on the predictability of market access for EVs produced at that facility to the United States.The U.S. decision at the July 1 joint review not to extend the USMCA in its current form means the agreement remains in effect but will move into annual reviews until the parties either agree to extend the pact or it expires in 2036. This will add uncertainty on hot-button issues such as rules of origin for autos, with the United States pushing for higher percentages of both North American- and U.S.-produced content, while considering placing a ceiling on Chinese content.More broadly, ongoing uncertainty over U.S. tariffs on Canadian imports complicates the landscape. For instance, on July 20, the White House announced new 50% tariffs on more than 500 categories of Canadian goods, citing discriminatory treatment of U.S. exports under Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act. With the tariffs scheduled to take effect in 30 days, Canadian leaders are considering their response. Notably, the White House asserts such tariffs apply to all covered goods, regardless of whether they are covered by USMCA. For auto supply chains that have avoided tariffs due to qualifying under USMCA, this could raise the risk of exposure to potential new tariffs. Without greater predictability, firms may be increasingly reluctant to invest in Canada and instead prioritize jurisdictions where the regulatory and trade environments are more certain. 

What lessons do the EU and Canadian experiences offer?

In the face of ongoing fuel price volatility and energy insecurity, Chinese EV investment could expand and diversify manufacturing capacity while advancing electrification and decarbonization. Many governments that are pursuing reindustrialization strategies face fiscal constraints and limited private sector appetite for large-scale manufacturing investments. Chinese firms, by contrast, often possess both capital and a willingness to invest in overseas production capacity. For host countries, this could reduce the need for large government subsidies and public expenditures.The challenge, of course, is structuring these arrangements in a way that maximizes benefits for host countries—in terms of emphasizing local employment, accessing advanced technologies, and supporting the broader manufacturing base, while managing risks related to supply chain dependencies and ensuring effective security safeguards—all while remaining attractive and practical for investors. In that regard, several observations regarding the initial responses by the EU and Canada to Chinese investment are worth consideration.First, the EU and Canada illustrate trade-offs between proposing strict conditions versus issuing flexible guidance, as well as the role of political signaling. The EU has focused on developing detailed frameworks and conditions for Chinese investment but largely after Chinese firms had already established a local presence in EVs and related sectors, and with little clarity on when firmer rules would go into effect. Canada, which still lacks flagship investments, has thus far taken a case-by-case approach guided by broad principles and political engagement. While strategies are still in the early phases of implementation, initial responses from Chinese firms can be assessed to gauge how they might suit host country objectives.The EU's more rules-based model could potentially provide greater predictability regarding policy objectives. However, it risks deterring investments through overly complex and demanding requirements, and Chinese officials have pushed back. It is unclear whether Chinese investors would be willing or permitted to comply with stricter conditions in practice, especially if they could provide strong revenue streams to cash-strapped firms. Moreover, while the IAA remains under legislative consideration, the prospect of new conditions appears to be encouraging some companies to accelerate new investments to avoid stricter future provisions. Given the relatively nascent stage of most facilities—with the earliest investments just now entering production—it remains to be seen whether those jurisdictions that have already welcomed investments, such as Spain and Hungary, will derive fewer or greater benefits than those that might only accept investments under stricter conditions.Canada's engagement-focused model has garnered strong public interest from Chinese investors, who may react more positively to high-level signaling that they are welcome in Canada. Putting forth flexible terms without strict thresholds could enable firms to pursue investment models that better suit their commercial interests and to more nimbly react to real-world political, technological, and market dynamics. But with no Chinese EV investments yet approved, it is difficult to gauge whether Canada’s vague guidance and screening mechanisms are robust enough to ensure that prospective deals serve Canada’s interests. Although stricter terms could risk stifling investor interest, some have argued that further safeguards are essential.Second, Beijing’s role in restricting outbound investment decisions by Chinese companies is becoming increasingly pronounced. Chinese regulators are exercising greater oversight regarding which overseas transactions receive approval, particularly in sectors deemed strategically important. Recent measures tightening controls on outbound investment, technology transfers, and data flows indicate that Chinese firms now operate with less discretion than in previous years. This may limit the range of overseas investment conditions that Beijing may be willing to permit, even if firms are keen to make deals.A new regulatory framework for overseas investments, which took effect on July 1, explicitly prohibits unauthorized cross-border transfers of personnel, expertise, and technical know-how, with broad discretion over which sectors are within its scope. These provisions come on the heels of two supply chain security decrees issued by the Chinese State Council in April, which, respectively, expanded the government’s authority to counter foreign sanctions and to take measures to safeguard critical supply chains. Notably, the measures empower authorities to impose exit restrictions on employees of foreign companies who participate in or facilitate the implementation of foreign sanctions targeting China, underscoring Beijing’s growing willingness to use administrative controls to advance national security and economic policy objectives.This dynamic may elevate the significance of political signaling. Chinese authorities are unlikely to support major investments in jurisdictions perceived as hostile to Chinese commercial interests. Host governments seeking Chinese investments, therefore, may need to provide stronger assurances that investments will be treated fairly and consistently to address concerns about unexpected changes in policy environments. In particular, Beijing’s more assertive behavior may dampen the prospects for Chinese EV firms to transfer technology to Western partners and limit the technologies that Chinese firms can use in foreign markets, especially given that a substantive tech transfer deal has yet to be realized.Third, China may increasingly insist on market access as a price for increased investments. Access to investments may depend partly on broader economic relations; countries that seek Chinese manufacturing investment while limiting Chinese imports may find that the two objectives are difficult to separate. Nations that seek investments from Chinese firms on favorable terms may find that progress is difficult unless they demonstrate some degree of continued openness to importing Chinese products. Canada’s approach is one example of this, whereby its effort to attract investments—which has yet to bear fruit—was paired with limited market access for Chinese EVs. The EU is increasingly facing similar questions.Fourth, regional market access may shape investment outcomes. The uncertainty surrounding the USMCA has incited hesitation among both Chinese and non-Chinese investors alike to move forward with plans in Canada. For Chinese firms, potential changes to how the USMCA treats rules of origin regarding Chinese content could limit U.S. market access, even if production occurs in Canada. U.S. trade chief Jamieson Greer has advocated for higher thresholds around U.S.-made parts and tightened rules on Chinese content. For countries such as Canada and Mexico that hope to attract investment but still rely on export markets, this is an extra challenge.To illustrate the complexity of the environment, last year, BYD canceled a plan to build an EV factory in Mexico due to concern over rising geopolitical tensions and shifting trade policies. While Guangzhou Automobile Group Co. (GAC) announced plans to begin assembling vehicles in Mexico in the second half of this year, the company said that vehicles built there would be limited to the Mexican market. Uncertainty is not just affecting Chinese companies—Japanese automaker Toyota recently announced it would spend US$3.6 billion to move more production from Mexico to Texas, within U.S. borders. Interest in acquiring existing manufacturing assets and establishing new production partnerships remains strong, but companies are increasingly cautious about committing capital before the region's future trade architecture becomes clearer.Policy debates in the EU and Canada over the past few months demonstrate continued interest in attracting Chinese investments, particularly in sectors that can support economic growth, manufacturing jobs, and the energy transition. In the EU, however, scrutiny has intensified due to concerns over de-industrialization, the prospect of a "China shock 2.0"—a surge of subsidized Chinese high-tech exports—and the long-term competitiveness of European industry. As a result, policymakers face growing pressure to reconcile the benefits of Chinese investment with broader economic and security concerns. In Canada, where the state of Chinese EV investment is more nascent, similar tensions are beginning to emerge.Both jurisdictions are still in the process of developing, refining, and solidifying their approaches. In the EU, questions remain regarding the adoption and implementation of the proposed IAA and revised Cybersecurity Act and potential further tariff and trade measures. Meanwhile, Canada is navigating uncertainty around the future of the USMCA while continuing to court Chinese firms on favorable terms, suggesting its industrial policy is still taking shape.The experiences of both Canada and the EU suggest that there is no single “right” approach to managing Chinese investment. Rather, what appears most important is the development of a framework that is consistent, transparent, and predictable, while promoting legitimate national interests. Given that many investments are long term in nature and require substantial planning and capital commitments, policy stability and regulatory clarity are likely to be essential for both investors and host jurisdictions.
